query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Plasma nitriding Ti-6Al-4V in an optimized NH3/N2 atmosphere (ratio 1:2) at 750 °C for 4 hours will form a thicker, well-adherent Ti–N compound layer that significantly increases surface hardness and improves wear resistance relative to the untreated alloy. This improvement is achieved by the formation of hard nitride layers that impede dislocation motion and surface abrasion.
generation.material_initial_state: Ti-6Al-4V alloy in its typical microstructure with baseline hardness around 400–450 HV and conventional wear characteristics.
generation.intervention: Plasma nitriding performed at 750 °C for 4 h in a gas mixture of NH3 and N2 at a 1:2 ratio.
generation.conditions: Effectiveness should be observed under room temperature abrasive sliding wear conditions (e.g., pin-on-disk test under an 8 N load) and under cyclic fatigue loading representative of structural service.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an outer compound layer composed of δ–TiN and ε–Ti2N, accompanied by an underlying nitrogen diffusion zone.
generation.mechanism: The nitride layers are much harder than the base alloy and act as a barrier to dislocation motion and surface abrasion. The compressive residual stresses and improved phase composition in the nitrided layer help delay crack initiation and reduce material removal during wear exposures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nitrided samples should exhibit a surface hardness increase by approximately 3–4 times compared to the untreated alloy and a significant reduction in wear rate (evidenced by lower weight loss and shallower wear scars) under the test conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated Ti-6Al-4V alloy with lower surface hardness (e.g., ~421 HV) and higher observed wear volume under similar loading.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect may diminish under very high contact stresses or if the increased surface roughness (a potential by-product of nitriding) leads to premature cracking. Optimization of nitriding parameters is thus critical.
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative improvements are supported by prior studies, the precise quantitative gains in hardness and wear resistance may vary with process specifics and sample variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti-6Al-4V alloy samples. Subject one set to plasma nitriding using the optimized NH3/N2 (1:2) process at 750 °C for 4 h while keeping the other set untreated. Conduct standardized pin-on-disk wear tests under an 8 N load as well as Vickers hardness measurements on both sets. Use scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to verify the formation and uniformity of the nitride layers.
measurements: Wear volume or weight loss after the wear test
Surface morphology and phase presence (via SEM and XRD) to confirm TiN/Ti2N formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the plasma nitrided samples do not show a statistically significant increase in surface hardness (at least 2× the baseline value) and a corresponding decrease in wear rate compared to the untreated samples, or if no clearly defined Ti–N compound layer is observed via microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The growth of the Ti-N compound layer was enhanced by the use of an NH3-N2 mixture during the plasma nitriding of the Ti6Al4V alloy. After nitriding at 750 °C for 4 h in an NH3-N2 (1:2) atmosphere, a Ti-N compound layer approximately 2 μm thick was formed on the Ti6Al4V alloy. The Ti-N compound layers are typically much harder than the titanium alloy substrate. In comparison to the un-nitrided titanium alloy, samples nitrided in an NH3-N2 mixture exhibited the complete elimination of stick–tear and plowing wear throughout the duration of the test, resulting in undetectable wear loss when in contact with bearing steel. The oxide layer formed on the wear track by the transfer of material from the counterpart steel ball reduced the average friction coefficient from approximately 0.55 to 0.30 under an 8N load. The formation of the Ti-N layer not only enhances the hardness and wear resistance of the titanium alloy but also increases its corrosion resistance.

Increased fatigue life of the plasma nitrided specimens in tests at higher stresses can be attributed to compressive residual stress in the nitride layers and in the nitrogen diffusion zone, thereby inhibiting crack nucleation at the alloy surface. This is in agreement with another study by Rodriguez et al. []. According to Farokhzadeh et al. [], the nitride layer reduces the extent of brittle failure on the specimen surface while the diffusion zone provides mechanical support. As per the study of Morita et al [], the formation of these layers after plasma nitriding increases the surface hardness of the alloy, which in turn increases the resistance to movement of dislocations and, as a consequence, increases the fatigue strength of the alloy. Rocha [], reported that delay in crack nucleation in plasma nitrided specimens is due to the difference in the Young modulus between the titanium alloy matrix (100 GPa) and the titanium nitrides formed on the plasma nitride surface (400 GPa). When high stresses are applied to the fragile nitride layer, it causes the nucleation and the growth of a crack in this layer.
